title: Sensor telemetry can be linked to the wearer's identity across sessions
description: Continuous submission of heart rate, step counts, GPS position, and timestamps from the wearer to the device enables the device/process to associate multiple observations with the same individual over time. Even if explicit identifiers are absent from a single sample, repeated location-time and physiological patterns can link records to one wearer.
assumptions: The wearable process stores or otherwise maintains continuity of telemetry over time, or can associate incoming samples with the same device/user account.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id chosen by best judgment; retrieved context confirms Linkability is applicable to ExternalEntity->Process flows, but did not include the exact L-node catalog.

title: Telemetry may identify the wearer directly or indirectly
description: GPS traces with timestamps, combined with heart rate and activity patterns, can reveal home/work locations and unique behavioral signatures that identify the wearer. The receiving process can therefore infer or confirm the user's identity from the submitted telemetry.
assumptions: The wearable process has access to sufficiently granular GPS/timestamp data or can combine telemetry with other available context.
uncertainty_note: Exact I-tree node id is selected by best judgment because the retrieved context did not provide the specific identifiability node list.

title: Continuous telemetry reveals sensitive behavior and health-related information
description: Heart rate, step counts, precise location, and timestamps expose personal aspects such as routines, exercise habits, sleep/wake cycles, visits to sensitive places, and possible health conditions. Disclosure of this data to the process exceeds ordinary observability and creates a privacy threat at collection time.
assumptions: The wearable process receives raw or granular telemetry rather than heavily aggregated values.
uncertainty_note: Exact D-tree node id is selected by best judgment; applicability of Detectability/Disclosure-related analysis to this flow is clear, but the retrieved context did not include the specific D threat-tree entries.

title: The device can detect the wearer's presence, movement, and activities continuously
description: Because the user is wearing the device continuously, the receiving process can detect whether the wearer is present, active, stationary, traveling, or absent at particular times. This makes otherwise non-obvious states and events detectable from the incoming telemetry stream.
assumptions: The process observes telemetry in near real time or with enough resolution to infer presence/activity states.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id chosen by best judgment; retrieved context confirms Dd applies to ExternalEntity->Process flows but not the exact subnode.

title: The wearer may be unaware they are continuously sharing personal telemetry
description: A wearer may not fully understand that continuous use of the device shares heart rate, steps, GPS position, and timestamps with the device process, nor the extent to which this data can reveal routines and health-related facts.
assumptions: Notices are absent, unclear, or insufficiently specific about always-on sensor collection and inference risks.

title: Collection of continuous telemetry may exceed the user's consent or expected purpose
description: Always-on capture of location, physiological, and activity data may go beyond what the wearer explicitly consented to or reasonably expects, especially if fine-grained GPS and timestamps are collected continuously rather than only when needed for a specific feature.
assumptions: Consent is bundled, ambiguous, or not granular enough to distinguish among sensor types, precision, retention, or collection frequency.
uncertainty_note: Exact Nc-tree node id is selected by best judgment because the retrieved context did not provide the consent/non-compliance subnodes.

title: Excessive disclosure of raw GPS traces and session data to the companion app
description: The wearable sends detailed exercise sessions, raw GPS traces, device identifier, and timestamps to the mobile app. If the app does not strictly need full-fidelity location traces or persistent device identifiers for its purpose, this flow discloses more personal data than necessary, including sensitive behavioral and location history.
assumptions: Assumes the companion app can function with reduced granularity, aggregation, or pseudonymization for at least some features.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id selected by best judgement for explicit, avoidable disclosure/minimality concerns; retrieved context supports Dd generally but does not provide a specific node-to-title mapping.

title: Linkability of batches to the same individual via persistent device id and timestamps
description: Including a stable device id together with repeated sensor batches and timestamps enables the companion app to link multiple exercise sessions and GPS traces to the same user over time. This can reveal long-term habits, routines, and mobility patterns beyond what may be necessary for a single sync event.
assumptions: Assumes the device id is stable across syncs and visible/usable by the app for correlation.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is best-effort based on standard linkability patterns; exact threat-tree numbering may differ.

title: Identifiability of the user from GPS traces and persistent identifiers
description: GPS traces, exercise routes, timestamps, and a device identifier can make the user directly or indirectly identifiable to the companion app. Home/work locations and routine paths are often sufficient to single out a person even without a real name in this flow.
assumptions: Assumes the app or its operators can access sufficiently precise route and timing data.
uncertainty_note: Specific node id is best-effort; applicability of identifiability is strong, but numbering may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Detectability of exercise events from sync timing and metadata
description: Even without inspecting full content, the presence, timing, size, and frequency of sync batches can allow the companion app to detect when exercise sessions occurred and infer activity intensity or duration. This exposes the occurrence of privacy-relevant events through metadata alone.
assumptions: Assumes the app can observe sync metadata such as batch arrival times, sizes, or frequency.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement for detectability via communication metadata; exact numbering may differ.

title: Insufficient user awareness or consent for syncing detailed sensor and location history
description: If users are not clearly informed that detailed exercise sessions, raw GPS traces, device id, and timestamps are synchronized from the wearable to the app, the flow may process personal data without valid, specific, and informed consent or another appropriate legal basis. Granular transparency is especially important for location data.
assumptions: Assumes consent/transparency for this specific sync is absent, bundled, unclear, or not sufficiently granular.
uncertainty_note: This is contingent on product notice/consent design, which is not provided in the prompt.

title: User may be unaware they are sharing highly sensitive health data with the app
description: When the wearer manually logs calorie intake, meals, and weight in the companion app, they are actively sharing personal and potentially health-related data. If the app does not clearly explain what is collected, for what purposes, and with whom it may be shared or combined, the user may provide this data without sufficient awareness.
assumptions: The app collects and stores the entered data and may use it beyond immediate on-screen display, such as syncing, analytics, profiling, or sharing with backend services.

title: Collection of meal and weight entries may exceed what is necessary for the stated purpose
description: The flow includes detailed food intake and weight information, which can reveal lifestyle patterns and health status. If the companion app requests or accepts more granular nutrition or body-metric data than needed for the user-facing function, the collection may not be compliant with data minimization and purpose-limitation expectations.
assumptions: The app's stated purpose may be broader wellness tracking, but the necessity of collecting all entered detail is not demonstrated from the flow alone.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement; exact LINDDUN Pro node id for non-compliance/data minimization may vary by version.

title: Manual diet and weight entries enable inference of sensitive health attributes
description: Calorie intake, meal logs, and weight entries can directly disclose or allow inference of sensitive attributes such as dieting behavior, obesity status, eating patterns, pregnancy, or medical conditions. Even though the user enters the data intentionally, the flow exposes information that is more privacy-sensitive than it may first appear.
assumptions: The app or downstream recipients can access the entered values and derive health-related conclusions from them.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may differ depending on the threat-tree version; this is a best-fit disclosure/inference node.

title: Repeated meal and weight submissions can be linked to a persistent user profile
description: Because entries are made through the companion app, multiple food and weight logs over time can be associated with the same app account, device, or session. This allows the app to link separate submissions into a longitudinal profile of the wearer’s habits and body changes.
assumptions: The companion app maintains a persistent identifier such as an account, device ID, or app profile.
uncertainty_note: Sub-node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context did not provide a specific linkability node id.

title: Excessive collection/storage of health logs in the store
description: The app writes detailed calorie intake, weight history, and exercise sessions into the health log store. This may constitute avoidable disclosure if the store persists more health data, granularity, or retention than is strictly necessary for the app’s purpose, increasing exposure of sensitive health-related personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the app may store full historical logs and fine-grained entries rather than only the minimum data needed for the stated service.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement for data minimization/excessive disclosure on a Process->DataStore flow; exact subnode label may vary across LINDDUN Pro editions.

title: Health log records may be identifiable to a specific user
description: The stored health logs can likely be tied to a particular account, device, or profile. Because weight history, calorie intake, and exercise sessions are highly personal and often longitudinal, the data in the store may directly identify or single out the individual behind the records.
assumptions: Assumes records are stored with an account identifier, device identifier, or other stable linkage needed to retrieve a user’s history.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subnode may differ; threat is that stored data is directly or indirectly identifying.

title: Longitudinal health logs enable linking of user activities over time
description: Writing repeated entries for calorie intake, weight, and exercise into one store creates a longitudinal profile. Entries from different days and categories can be linked to the same person or profile, allowing correlation of behaviors and trends over time beyond what may be necessary for the immediate feature.
assumptions: Assumes the datastore groups multiple log entries under the same user/profile or stable pseudonym.
uncertainty_note: Subnode selected by best judgement for linkability via common identifier or longitudinal record aggregation.

title: Stored health logs may allow inference of sensitive attributes
description: Even if individual fields seem routine, the combination of calorie intake, weight trends, and exercise sessions can reveal sensitive patterns such as medical conditions, pregnancy, eating disorders, religious practices, or lifestyle characteristics. Persisting these combined logs in the store increases detectability of such sensitive facts.
assumptions: Assumes the data can be queried or analyzed together as a coherent history.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode may vary; threat concerns inference/detectability of sensitive traits from stored behavioral and health data.

title: Storage of health logs may exceed user consent or expected purpose
description: Users may expect health logging for immediate app functionality, but not indefinite storage, secondary analytics, or broader reuse. If the app writes these logs to persistent storage without sufficiently specific consent, transparent purpose limitation, or an easy way to withdraw/adjust preferences, the flow can create non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes consent, purpose limitation, retention, or withdrawal controls are not clearly aligned with this persistent storage operation.
uncertainty_note: Subnode chosen by best judgement for consent/purpose-limitation compliance threat on data storage; exact node label may differ.

title: Excessive retention of precise location history
description: Writing raw GPS traces with timestamps to the location history store can disclose more personal data than necessary if precision, sampling rate, or retention period exceed what is strictly needed for the app's purpose. Historical location trails are highly sensitive and can reveal home/work, routines, and visits to sensitive places.
assumptions: The store keeps precise, longitudinal location traces rather than immediately aggregating, truncating, or aging them out according to a defined purpose limitation policy.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best-fit judgement for unnecessary/overbroad storage disclosure; the retrieved context confirms Dd applicability to Process->DataStore but does not provide the exact subnode text.

title: Over-collection of location and temporal metadata on write
description: The app may write full GPS coordinates plus exact timestamps for every trace even where coarser location, lower frequency, or event-based collection would suffice. This explicit collection and transfer into storage is an avoidable disclosure of personal data under data minimization principles.
assumptions: The business function could operate with less granular location data or fewer samples than are currently written.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode citation is approximate; threat is grounded in LINDDUN Data Disclosure/minimality for the flow.

title: Longitudinal location records enable identity inference
description: Even if the stored traces are not explicitly labeled with a real-world identity, a history of GPS points with timestamps can often be linked back to an individual by inferring home/work addresses, routines, or co-location patterns. Storing such data therefore creates a realistic identifiability threat.
assumptions: Records are associated with a device, account, pseudonym, or otherwise stable pattern over time.
uncertainty_note: Subnode chosen as a best-fit identifiability/inference node; retrieved context does not enumerate I subnodes.

title: Stored trace patterns allow linkage across sessions and contexts
description: A persistent location history store can link multiple app sessions and events to the same person or device over time. Repeated writes of timestamped GPS traces strengthen the ability to correlate records across days, devices, or datasets, undermining unlinkability.
assumptions: The store uses a persistent identifier, account key, device identifier, or another stable handle to append traces over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is an approximate best-fit for linkability due to persistent longitudinal records.

title: Presence at sensitive places becomes detectable from stored history
description: Location traces with timestamps can reveal whether a user visited or was near sensitive places such as clinics, religious sites, protests, workplaces, or home. This makes otherwise private attributes and activities detectable from the stored dataset.
assumptions: Stored coordinates remain precise enough to map to venues or areas of interest.
uncertainty_note: Exact detectability subnode is approximate; applicability is strong because precise geolocation histories directly expose presence patterns.

title: Location-history storage may exceed user expectations or valid consent scope
description: Persistently storing timestamped GPS traces may be non-compliant if users were not clearly informed, did not freely consent where required, or cannot exercise controls such as deletion and retention choices. The privacy risk arises at the point this flow commits the data to long-term storage.
assumptions: The service relies on consent, notice, or purpose limitation obligations for collecting and storing location history.
uncertainty_note: This is a policy/compliance-oriented privacy threat inferred from the nature of location-history storage; exact legal basis is system-specific.

title: Cross-session health logs enable linkage of records to the same individual
description: The analytics service reads calorie, weight, and exercise logs across sessions for health-condition analysis. Combining these recurring measurements over time can link multiple sessions and records to the same person, creating a longitudinal profile beyond isolated log entries.
assumptions: The service can access persistent identifiers, account linkage, or stable quasi-identifiers that let it associate records across sessions.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id chosen by best judgement for linkability via longitudinal correlation; the provided context did not include the specific L threat-tree node mapping.

title: Health-condition analysis increases identifiability from quasi-identifying health patterns
description: Weight trends, exercise habits, and calorie logs can form a distinctive behavioral and physiological pattern. When the analytics service reads these data together across sessions, the resulting pattern may make the data subject identifiable, especially when combined with other available context.
assumptions: The analytics service or connected components may have access to auxiliary data or stable user context that can single out individuals.
uncertainty_note: Specific I-tree node id is based on best judgement; exact node numbering may differ in the source threat tree.

title: Health-condition inference reveals sensitive medical information beyond raw logs
description: Analyzing calorie, weight, and exercise logs for health-condition analysis can infer sensitive information such as obesity risk, eating disorders, pregnancy, chronic conditions, or other health states that are more privacy-sensitive than the original inputs.
assumptions: The service derives or exposes health-condition conclusions from the underlying logs.
uncertainty_note: Threat clearly applies, but the exact D-tree node id is selected by best judgement because the retrieved context did not include inference-specific node numbering.

title: Analytics service may process more health-log data than necessary
description: The flow transfers calorie, weight, and exercise logs across sessions to the analytics service. Because these are sensitive health-related data, reading the full longitudinal log set for analysis may disclose more personal data to the service than is strictly necessary if only aggregated, recent, or subset data would suffice.
assumptions: Some analyses could be performed with minimized attributes, reduced history, or aggregated features rather than full raw logs.
uncertainty_note: Dd.1.1 is chosen by best judgement for unnecessary/avoidable disclosure to an internal recipient; the retrieved context emphasized minimality but did not provide exact node numbering.

title: Secondary use of health logs for condition analysis may exceed user consent or expectations
description: Users may have provided calorie, weight, and exercise logs for tracking and coaching, but this flow uses them across sessions for health-condition analysis. If that analytic purpose was not specifically communicated and consented to, the processing may violate consent, purpose-limitation, or expectation boundaries.
assumptions: The original collection notice or consent did not explicitly cover cross-session health-condition analysis of these logs.
uncertainty_note: Threat applicability depends on the stated purpose and consent model; exact Nc-tree node id is based on best judgement.

title: Cross-session location history enables linking of records and behaviors to the same individual
description: By querying historical location data across sessions, the analytics service can correlate multiple observations over time into a single behavioral profile. This makes it possible to link otherwise separate sessions, trips, and visits to the same person, increasing re-identification risk.
assumptions: Location history records are associated with a stable device, account, pseudonym, or other recurring identifier that allows cross-session correlation.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best-fit judgement for linkability because the retrieved context did not include the detailed LINDDUN threat tree.

title: Daily routine and movement patterns may make the user identifiable
description: Derived daily routines and movement patterns can uniquely characterize an individual, especially when home/work locations, commute patterns, or frequent visits are inferred. Even if raw data is pseudonymous, the analytics output may permit singling out and identification of the user.
assumptions: The service derives sufficiently granular patterns such as regular start/end locations, frequented venues, or distinctive mobility habits.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is a best-fit estimate for identifiability from quasi-identifying behavioral patterns.

title: Routine analysis detects presence at sensitive places and times
description: Analyzing location history across sessions reveals when a person was present at particular places and how often, exposing behaviors such as visits to medical, religious, political, or other sensitive locations. This enables detection of private activities and habits beyond what is strictly necessary for many analytics purposes.
assumptions: Location data is precise enough to associate visits with meaningful places or categories of places.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree mapping for detectability was not provided in context; node id is best-fit.

title: Analytics service processes more location history than necessary to derive patterns
description: Querying location history across sessions for routine inference risks excessive disclosure of personal data to the analytics service. The full longitudinal history can reveal sensitive lifestyle information, while a more privacy-preserving design might use reduced precision, shorter retention windows, aggregation, or on-device computation.
assumptions: The analytics service has access to raw or fine-grained historical location traces rather than minimized or pre-aggregated data.
uncertainty_note: The applicability of data disclosure is strong here under the minimality principle cited in context, but the exact subtree id is best-fit.

title: Cross-session routine profiling may exceed users' expectations of location-data use
description: Users may not expect stored location history to be retrospectively analyzed across sessions to infer daily routines and movement patterns. If this secondary analysis is insufficiently transparent or not meaningfully controllable, users can become unaware of how their data is being used.
assumptions: The original user-facing notice or consent did not clearly describe longitudinal behavioral profiling from location history.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness is inferred from the described secondary analytics purpose; exact tree-node id is approximate.

title: Routine profiling may be incompatible with purpose limitation or consent constraints
description: Using historical location data across sessions to derive daily routines may go beyond the originally specified purpose for collecting location data, especially if the initial purpose was operational or session-based. This creates a risk that processing is not compliant with purpose limitation, data minimization, or consent requirements.
assumptions: The system collected location history for a narrower purpose than long-term behavioral analytics, or jurisdictional rules require a distinct legal basis for such profiling.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on the actual stated purpose, legal basis, and jurisdiction; tree-node id is best-fit.

title: Inference output reveals or confirms the user's identity-sensitive health status
description: The analytics service sends inferred health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags to the mobile app. Even if raw inputs were previously less explicit, these derived outputs can directly identify the user with respect to sensitive health characteristics by confirming or making deducible specific conditions, habits, or risk categories.
assumptions: The insights are tied to an individual user account/device and concern special-category health data or closely related inferences.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort because the retrieved context gives the Identifying category but not the detailed subtree.

title: Sensitive inferred health insights may be disclosed to unintended recipients via the app flow
description: This flow carries highly sensitive inferred analytics results from the health analytics service to the companion app. If the transfer, routing, session binding, or in-app delivery is incorrect, another party could gain access to health-condition risk indicators, summaries, or trend flags that were intended only for the data subject.
assumptions: The app may run on shared or compromise-prone devices, and message delivery depends on account/session/device association being correct.
uncertainty_note: Detailed D subtree citation is approximate; the risk clearly falls under disclosure of sensitive inferred data on this process-to-process flow.

title: Returned analytics insights enable linkage across health events and behavior patterns
description: Routine summaries and trend flags can act as stable, distinctive signals that allow records or observations about the same user to be linked across time, features, or datasets. This can expose longitudinal behavior patterns and correlations beyond what the user expects from isolated measurements.
assumptions: The app stores or displays multiple analytics returns over time, or combines them with other user/account context.
uncertainty_note: Specific L subtree node is best-effort due to missing detailed linkage nodes in retrieved context.

title: Users may be unaware that the app receives and presents sensitive inferred health conclusions
description: The flow returns not just raw readings but derived risk indicators and trend assessments. If the app does not clearly explain that these are inferred outputs, their meaning, confidence, and downstream use, users may not understand the nature and privacy impact of the processing.
assumptions: The mobile app is the user-facing point where notice and explanation should be provided.
uncertainty_note: Exact U subtree node is approximate; threat selection is based on lack of transparency/awareness around inferred data.

title: Delivering inferred health-risk insights without adequate privacy-risk governance may create non-compliance
description: Because this flow transfers special-category inferred health information to the app, failures in transparency, access control, minimization, or justification for processing can create compliance gaps. In particular, inadequate cybersecurity and privacy risk management for sensitive inferences may violate legal or best-practice obligations.
assumptions: Applicable obligations exist for health-related inferred data, including transparency, security, and lawful processing requirements.
uncertainty_note: Nc.3 is directly supported by the retrieved context, but the exact legal obligations depend on jurisdiction and system scope.

title: Sensitive inferred health indicators may be exposed on the dashboard to unintended viewers
description: The app sends trend views and inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk indicators to the user's device for display. If the dashboard is visible to shoulder surfers, appears in screenshots/screen recordings, or is surfaced in OS previews/notifications, highly sensitive health inferences can be disclosed to people other than the intended user.
assumptions: The mobile app or device may display this information in contexts where others can observe it, and the inferred indicators qualify as sensitive personal data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best-fit LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure threat-tree semantics for disclosure during legitimate output/display; exact node label may vary by repository version.

title: User may be unaware that the dashboard reveals inferred condition risk signals
description: The dashboard presents trends and inferred condition indicators. A user may not realize that the shown results are privacy-sensitive inferences derived from their underlying data, how such inferences were generated, or the implications of sharing the screen or showing the app to others. This creates unawareness about the privacy impact of receiving and potentially further sharing these personal data.
assumptions: The app does not clearly explain that these are inferred health-related assessments and does not sufficiently warn about their sensitivity or downstream sharing implications.
uncertainty_note: U.1.2 explicitly concerns unawareness in user sharing contexts; here it is applied because displaying the data to the user can enable onward sharing or exposure. Fit is reasonable but somewhat interpretive.

title: Displaying inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals without adequate safeguards may create compliance issues
description: This flow communicates special-category or otherwise highly sensitive health inferences to the user. If the app lacks appropriate transparency, lawful basis/consent handling, data minimization, accuracy controls, or protections against incidental exposure, the display may contribute to non-compliance with privacy and health-data obligations.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy treats these inferences as regulated sensitive personal data and requires heightened transparency and protection.
uncertainty_note: Nc node naming can differ across LINDDUN Pro materials; 'Nc.1' is used as a best-judgment placeholder for a general compliance threat linked to disclosure/unawareness around sensitive inferred health data.

title: Excessive disclosure of full health and location dataset to third-party cloud host
description: The flow sends analytics data, models, and the full health and location dataset to a third-party cloud hosting provider for hosting and replication. This may disclose more personal data than is strictly necessary for the hosting purpose, especially given the sensitivity of health data and the identifiability/location dimension.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud provider is a separate third party and that not all fields of the full dataset are strictly required in identifiable form for hosting/replication.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement based on LINDDUN Pro disclosure/minimality structure; exact sub-node citation may differ.

title: Disclosure through replication and secondary storage at cloud provider
description: Replication at the cloud provider increases the number of copies, storage locations, and administrative domains in which the full health and location dataset exists. This broadens exposure and may create avoidable disclosure to additional personnel, subprocessors, regions, or backup systems beyond the primary hosting need.
assumptions: Assumes cloud replication may involve multiple regions, backup systems, or subprocessors and that these extra copies are not all strictly necessary or transparently governed.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id is approximate; grounded in avoidable third-party/secondary disclosure via replication.

title: Transfer of special-category health and location data to cloud provider may lack valid legal basis or purpose limitation
description: Sending the full health and location dataset to a third-party host may be incompatible with the original purposes, exceed the declared processing scope, or lack an adequate legal basis/processor arrangement for special-category and location data. This creates a non-compliance risk attached to the disclosure flow itself.
assumptions: Assumes the dataset contains personal data subject to data protection law and that contractual, purpose-limitation, cross-border, or processor-control requirements may not be fully satisfied.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro non-compliance sub-node may vary; threat is included because the flow explicitly transfers sensitive data to a third party.

title: Hosting and replication by third party may be insufficiently transparent to data subjects
description: Data subjects may not reasonably expect that their full health and location dataset, along with derived analytics models, are hosted and replicated by a third-party cloud provider. If this transfer and its implications are not clearly communicated, the flow creates an unawareness threat.
assumptions: Assumes notices/consent records may not explicitly mention third-party cloud hosting, replication, retention, or international storage implications.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; included due to likely opacity of third-party hosting/replication for sensitive data.

title: Replicated cloud-hosted dataset enables stronger identifiability of individuals
description: The transfer includes the full health and location dataset, whose combination of attributes can strongly identify or single out individuals. Hosting and replication preserve or amplify identifiability if the data is stored in directly identifiable or readily re-identifiable form at the cloud provider.
assumptions: Assumes the dataset contains direct identifiers or quasi-identifiers and is not robustly de-identified before transfer.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifiability sub-node is best-judgement; threat applies because full health plus location data is highly identifying.

title: Cloud-hosted health and location data can link records and activities across contexts
description: A full dataset containing both health and location information, together with analytics artifacts and replicated storage, can enable linking the same individual across services, time periods, devices, or datasets. The cloud provider environment may facilitate such cross-context correlation if common identifiers, metadata, or model features are retained.
assumptions: Assumes persistent identifiers, account metadata, timestamps, device IDs, or stable pseudonyms are included or inferable in the hosted data or models.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is approximate; included because combined health/location datasets are highly linkable even when partially pseudonymized.
